data.title: Gasoline refining margins inch down from recent highs
data.description:
Northwest European gasoline refining margins inched down at $60.20 a barrel on Friday, still hovering near record highs reached during the 2022 energy crisis, as supplies remained tight despite an increase in regional inventories.

  • About 4 metric tons of gasoline E5 barges traded, with MB and BP selling to Gunvor and Trafigura.

  • A further 4 tons of gasoline E10 barges traded, with ATL and Equinor selling to Varo and Exxon.

  • Nigeria's Dangote Group is planning to price the initial public offering of its refinery unit at 525 naira ($0.40) per share, potentially raising about $1.5 billion, two people with direct knowledge of the deal told Reuters on Friday.

  • Gasoline stocks independently held in the Amsterdam-Rotterdam-Antwerp refining and storage hub rose by nearly 18% on the week, data from Dutch consultancy Insights Global showed on Thursday.

  • Gasoline stocks rose to 885,000 metric tons on lower exports to other regions, Insights Global analyst Rick Veringmeier said, adding that blending activity for the motor fuel was also rising.

  • "In the short term, EBOB spreads may have further upside to go, particularly over the next two weeks as we roll into the September window seeing renewed buying activity in E5 barges, with inventories remaining tight," said Sparta Commodities analyst Nikolas Plonski.

  • U.S. gasoline stocks fell by 1.2 million barrels to 205.7 million barrels in the week to August 28, according to the Energy Information Administration.

data.title: U.S. Labor Market Still Tight for Recent Grads — Market Talk
data.description: The better-than-expected jobs report shows the labor market is solid for current workers, but college graduates are still having a hard time finding work, Fifth Third Commercial Bank's Bill Adams says in a note. The rate of unemployment among recent grads in August was the highest since 2014, according to Adams. The cohort's unemployment rates are highly seasonal and spike every summer, but this past month had 12% higher unemployment than August 2025, he says. The weak hiring for grads is due in part to AI's impact on the job market, Adams says. (dean.seal@wsj.com)

data.title: Nymex Overview: Crude Futures Moving Lower but Set for Weekly Gains — OPIS
data.description:
Crude oil and ULSD futures were moving lower Friday morning while gasoline futures were seeing gains ahead of the long Labor Day holiday weekend.

Despite the losses, crude futures contracts are on track to end the week with solid gains amid the flare up in fighting between the U.S. and Iran.

There was divergence in losses for front-month and next-month oil futures, with the NYMEX October West Texas Intermediate crude contract down $1.08 to $90.22/bbl at about 11 a.m. ET while the November contract was moving lower by 55cts to $87.64/bbl.

The November ICE Brent crude contract was trading 35cts lower at $95.17/bbl while December prices were off by 6cts to $91.57/bbl.

ULSD futures prices are getting much attention as the retail price of diesel in the U.S. rose to record levels Thursday. The October ULSD contract was down 5.95cts to $4.5341/gal and November prices were 5.07cts lower to $4.3725/gal.

RBOB futures prices were seeing solid gains heading into the afternoon, with the October contract rising by 4.41cts to $3.179/gal and November prices trading 2.19cts higher to $2.9808/gal.

Crude prices are set to end the week about $7/bbl higher while the front-month ULSD contract is on track for an increase of about 17cts. A change in RVP requirements at the beginning of the month to a less-expensive winter blend means that the front-month RBOB contract is about 31cts below last Friday's settlement.

Motorists taking to the roads for the Labor Day weekend are facing record fuel prices, with the national average price of regular unleaded at $4.1474/gal, easily surpassing the $3.83/gal that had been the highest ever for the holiday weekend. Retail diesel prices were averaging $5.85/gal Friday, about 3.5cts/gal higher than the previous all-time high of $5.8159/gal set in 2022.

("EDX Medical" or the "Company")

Director/PDMR shareholdings in the Company

CAMBRIDGE, UK: EDX Medical Group plc ("EDX Medical", the "Company" or the "Group"), which develops and supplies innovative digital diagnostic products and services for the early detection and treatment of major diseases, has received notification of the following reductions in shareholding as a result of the dilution from the recent equity fundraising.

Dr Michael Hudson, chief executive officer, and his persons closely associated, continues to hold a total of 20,650,000 ordinary shares which now represent 4.79% of the share capital of the Company.

Professor Sir Christopher Evans, founder and chief scientific officer, continues to hold 136,220,293 ordinary shares which now represent 31.58% of the share capital of the Company. This total includes an additional 58,770 ordinary shares compared to previous notifications as a result of purchases in 2025 and January 2026 that were made on his behalf but that were not notified at the time due to an administrative oversight.

The directors of the Company accept responsibility for the contents of this announcement.

About EDX Medical Group plc

EDX Medical Group plc is listed on the AIM market (TIDM: EDX). The Company develops and supplies class-leading clinical diagnostics products and services.

EDX Medical was founded by Professor Sir Christopher Evans, OBE, a medical and life sciences entrepreneur with more than 30 years of experience, together with CEO, Dr Mike Hudson. The Company operates its own laboratory facilities in Cambridge UK, and has strategic product and technology partnerships with leading life sciences and healthcare organisations. Products and services are available to healthcare providers and individuals, and the Company also offers an employee health screening programme to employers.

By translating clinical insights into pragmatic solutions combining advanced biological and digital technologies, EDX Medical seeks to cost effectively improve the early detection and characterisation of disease to enable personalised treatment. Early disease detection and personal treatment optimisation is considered to be the most impactful way of improving patient outcomes.

data.title: What's Moving Markets Today? — WSJ
data.description:
By Shradha Dinesh

The Dow Jones Industrial Average, S&P 500 and Nasdaq edged lower today as a strong August jobs report provided another datapoint for Federal Reserve policy expectations. Also, diesel prices hit a record high, and another retail brand, Lululemon Athletica, took an earnings hit.

Here is what is driving the markets today:

Fed hike risk returns on August jobs: Job growth is strong, according to August's employment report. That removes one obstacle to a Fed interest rate hike after expectations softened yesterday on remarks by Fed governor Christopher Waller. The odds of a Fed rate hike this month have now increased to around 60-40 in favor of a rate hike, according to CME FedWatch. This is up from a coin-flip chance yesterday.

Diesel shocks: The latest commodity to hit fresh records? Diesel. The U.S.'s war on Iran propelled the national average price of diesel to $5.850 a gallon Friday, the highest on record, up from $3.712 a year ago. Disruptions to Strait of Hormuz traffic have stifled global exporters of refined fuels, boosting demand for American producers. Higher prices have followed.

Lululemon earnings snag: The activewear retailer reported diminished sales in the Americas and revised down its earnings estimates through the year-end. Executives attributed dented sales to negative online narratives about the brand, several product launch misses and pressure from competitors such as Alo and Vuori.

data.title: Credit Bureau, Fair Isaac Shares Retreat as FHFA Chief Pulte Slams Industry
data.description:
By Elias Schisgall

Shares of major credit bureaus and Fair Isaac fell after a top federal housing regulator criticized their prices and the reliance on FICO scores in mortgage lending.

Shares of Fair Isaac, the company behind the FICO score, were down 18% to $922.67 in Friday morning trading. Equifax's stock was off 7.9% at $174.26, TransUnion was down 8% at $78.09, and shares in Experian retreated 4.8% to $37.91 in over-the-counter trading.

Federal Housing Finance Agency Director Bill Pulte took to X on Thursday night to accuse Fair Isaac of operating a monopoly over credit scores. He said he was directing Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac to approve all lenders using the rival VantageScore model.

The agency had previously greenlit the use of VantageScore 4.0 last summer, according to The Wall Street Journal.

Pulte also accused the three credit bureaus--Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion--of "overcharging Americans for far too long" and stringing along regulators.

"We are seriously considering bi-merge, and stronger solutions (SAFER and SOUNDER)," Pulte wrote in one post. "We will not allow companies to take advantage of American consumers."

The companies named by Pulte did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

"We have asked the CEOs of the Credit Bureaus for solutions but they seem more intent on "happy talk", tapping us along with meetings, and operating as "cartel-like", which is not in the best interest of American homeowners," Pulte said in another post. "Time for a change."

Write to Elias Schisgall at elias.schisgall@wsj.com

data.title: The 33-Year-Old AI Hotshot Taking Silicon Valley Swagger Back to Beijing — WSJ
data.description:
By Angel Au-Yeung

Many of China's brightest computer engineering students come to the U.S. for its educational opportunities and often stay, shaping tech culture from teaching positions at prestigious schools or senior roles at companies big and small.

Yang Zhilin wanted to go home.

Yang, whose company recently sent jitters through global markets after releasing a powerful AI model, wanted to see if he could bring what he found in America back to China.

His Ph.D. adviser at Carnegie Mellon University-renowned computer scientist Ruslan Salakhutdinov-thought it was a bad idea.

"That's not what I would have done in his shoes," Salakhutdinov said. Salakhutdinov was well aware that Apple wanted to recruit Yang. "He was on the trajectory upwards. That's just not what I would have done."

Yang's gamble is starting to pay off. The 33 years old is the co-founder and chief executive of Moonshot AI, one of China's top AI labs. His startup's latest private funding round values it at $50 billion, and confidentially submitted an application for an initial public offering to Hong Kong's stock exchange, The Wall Street Journal has reported. Moonshot's Kimi family of models become a household name among a global class of software engineers globally, the power users driving the AI boom.

He's infusing his Beijing-based startup with Western flair. Founded in early 2023, Moonshot has a Chinese name that translates to "The Dark Side of the Moon," a nod to Yang's Pink Floyd superfandom. Moonshot eschews titles and hierarchy, a relatively unusual practice at a Chinese company and one Yang sees as essential to get rid of red tape. "Direct communication" is his personal motto.

"I think a lot of us who did grad school in the U.S. would share this kind of openness and defiance to hierarchy and authority," said Peng Qi, an executive at a U.S. tech company Uniphore. Qi came to America to get his Ph.D. in computer science at Stanford University, and worked with Yang on research projects while interning together at Meta Platforms.

Moonshot's roughly 300 employees sometimes wear slippers in the office and step into conference rooms named after bands and musicians including Led Zeppelin, Metallica, Queen, Prince and Bob Dylan. A leather jacket and a pair of black cowboy boots sit on an office wall display.

The adoption of Silicon Valley swagger in China is part of a fascinating cultural exchange happening in both places. Many Chinese nationals are among a small group of core employees building AI systems at the biggest U.S. companies, including at OpenAI, Meta and elsewhere. Experts in training models, machine learning and engineering, they are some of the most prized AI employees in the world.

Meanwhile, some American startups, racing to build the next generation of trillion-dollar companies, have also embraced the "9-9-6" schedule-a grueling timetable of working from 9 a.m. to 9 p.m., six days a week-that has its origins in China.

Yang's blend of Western culture in a Chinese startup is working. In July, Yang's Moonshot released Kimi K3, the newest version of its flagship model that some AI researchers say is nearly as good as U.S.-born models for a fraction of the cost.

Kimi was one of a wave of Chinese labs that are open-weight, which means they are generally cheaper and allow for more customization than the closed-source models coming out of Anthropic and OpenAI.

The increasing popularity of such models has turned the AI race upside-down, threatening the massive valuations of Anthropic and OpenAI as they prepare for public listings as early as this fall. Some executives and government officials have suggested a ban on such Chinese open models, suggesting their leaps forward have been driven by a practice called "distillation," using massive volumes of outputs from advanced U.S. AI models to train their models.

Yang and Moonshot declined to comment. A company spokeswoman pointed to Yang's comments in recent years in Chinese publications.

"A hotshot"

Born in the southern province of Guangdong, Yang started intensive training in programming when he was 17 years old and competed in China's National Olympiad in Informatics.

He got into Tsinghua University, often called the "MIT of China" and a critical launchpad for the careers of many top Chinese AI researchers in the U.S.

As an undergrad, he formed a rock band, where he played drums and wrote songs. The band was called Splay, named after "splay tree," a computer science term for a type of data structure, according to the band's surviving old website.

At Tsinghua, Yang studied under Tang Jie, a prolific professor who would go on to start Z.AI, a top Chinese lab that competes with Moonshot today.

The two co-authored a number of broadly cited research papers on machine-learning that were presented at prestigious international conferences, which is unusual for an undergraduate, said William Cohen, a professor of machine learning at Carnegie Mellon who co-advised Yang with Salakhutdinov.

"He was already pretty well-known in the community," said Cohen, who remembers meeting Yang when Yang toured Carnegie Mellon as a prospective student. "He was sort of like this hotshot from the top school in China and was clearly a catch for whoever was able to recruit him."

Yang started at Carnegie Mellon in 2015. Despite being younger than other Ph.D. candidates-he came straight from undergrad-both Cohen and Salakhutidinov said he required less hand-holding than others and was able to quickly define his projects and research ideas.

Bhuwan Dhingra, a fellow Ph.D. candidate at the time, remembered Yang as friendly but reserved. While he learned very little of Yang's personal life, he was often impressed by his intellect.

"There were problems that people spend weeks figuring out, oftentimes never ending on a solution," he said. "But Zhilin would solve it without spending anything thinking about it. He'd just go on a blackboard and write out a solution. I still think of that a lot," said Dhingra, who now teaches at Duke University.

Toward the end of his stint at Carnegie Mellon, he interned at Google Brain, the company's pioneering AI deep-learning research team.

In 2019, Yang co-authored two research papers with Google Brain founding member Quoc V. Le about machine learning that has over 20,000 citations today. "It's highly unlikely for Ph.D. students to publish papers like this," said Salakhutdinov.

Salakhutdinov calls Yang one of the top students he's encountered. Other students he has mentored include Jimmy Ba, co-founder of Elon Musk's artificial intelligence venture xAI, and Devendra Chaplot, a founding team member of Mistral AI and Thinking Machines Lab.

In Yang's career discussions at the end of his Ph.D., he made it clear to Cohen and Salakhutidinov he was set on returning to China to build a startup. It was a surprise to both, but especially Salakhutdinov.

Of all of Salakhutdinov's Chinese national students, only two have elected to go back to China - Yang being one of them. "He never even did a proper job search," he said.

But to Dhingra, this wasn't entirely surprising. Dhingra recalled talking to Yang about his research papers he had published while at Google as an intern. "He told me that he's confident that if somebody gives him the money and the compute, he could build something that was going to beat all the models from OpenAI and Google," said Dhingra. "He was very confident in his abilities."

data.title: Grundig Unveils New Product Lineup at IFA 2026, Marking a New Phase in Strategic Partnership
data.description:
BERLIN, Sept. 4, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Grundig, the premium European home appliance brand, unveiled a new lineup spanning key categories including TVs, refrigerators, washer-dryer sets and air conditioners at IFA 2026. The event also marked a new phase in the strategic partnership between Beko, Grundig's parent company, and Changhong, following the licensing of the Grundig brand to Changhong in selected product categories and markets. The event presented the brand's latest product portfolio and marked the beginning of its next phase under the partnership.

By leveraging Changhong's R&D, manufacturing, and supply chain strengths alongside Grundig's deep European heritage and market presence, the partnership will further expand opportunities for Grundig in Europe and other international markets. Drawing on Grundig's deep-rooted legacy, design philosophy and market presence, the two companies will further integrate their respective capabilities and brand strengths, supporting Grundig's product innovation, brand operations and long-term growth in key markets.

Grundig's new lineup marks a key partnership milestone. The AURORA 100 flagship TV features RGB Micro-Focusing LED chips, OD8 ultra-narrow light-control technology and 9,720 independently controlled dimming zones. Its slim 39-millimeter profile and AI-powered Aurora Light Wings deliver an immersive audiovisual experience that combines vivid picture quality with a design that complements the home. The Space Pro refrigerator series pairs a slim 599mm depth with a spacious 600L capacity and a -3.5°C Fresh Zone. Rounding out the collection are integrated washer-dryers with 45°C heat-pump drying and AI-powered air conditioners featuring fresh-air circulation and purification.

From product design to the user experience, Grundig has consistently embraced its brand tagline, "It starts at home", designing appliances that blend naturally into living spaces. The newly launched products continue Grundig's focus on design, quality and smart experiences while incorporating localized innovation tailored to lifestyles in different markets.

Grundig's presence at IFA 2026 marks not only an important milestone in the brand's history, but also a significant step toward putting the Changhong-Beko strategic partnership into practice. Looking ahead, both companies will leverage their combined expertise in technology, branding, and market operations to drive product innovation. Together, they aim to expand Grundig's global footprint, offering modern home solutions that blend quality, innovation, and design.

John and his team, The Hall Wealth Management Group, join the UBS Pacific Northwest Market, managed by Rob Giordano.

“We are excited to welcome John to UBS in Bellevue,” said Cy Aleman, Market Director in the Pacific Northwest. “John is widely respected for his industry experience, thoughtful advice and unwavering commitment to his clients.”

“John is a tremendous addition to our branch and the broader Pacific Northwest Market,” said Michelle Fenske, Senior Market Director in Bellevue. “His depth of experience and sophisticated approach to wealth management align exceptionally well with the high standards we uphold for the families and institutions we serve.”

John joins UBS from Merrill in Bellevue. Known for his client-first approach, he is dedicated to understanding each client’s individual goals and helping individuals and families build greater financial confidence. Together with The Hall Wealth Management Group, he provides comprehensive financial planning, investment management, tax-aware wealth strategies and business succession planning, while developing trusted, long-term client relationships.

The Hall Wealth Management Group also includes Financial Advisor Aaron Marshall and Client Associate Jennifer Teddy. Aaron Marshall brings a relationship-focused approach to helping individuals and families make informed financial decisions. Jennifer Teddy brings more than 20 years of financial services experience and is dedicated to delivering an exceptional client experience.

Notes to Editors

About UBS
UBS is a leading and truly global wealth manager and the leading universal bank in Switzerland. It also provides diversified asset management solutions and focused investment banking capabilities. UBS manages 7.3 trillion dollars of invested assets as per the second quarter 2026. UBS helps clients achieve their financial goals through personalized advice, solutions and products. Headquartered in Zurich, Switzerland, the firm is operating in more than 50 markets around the globe. UBS Group shares are listed on the SIX Swiss Exchange and the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE).
